WA-2025-SB5925.aiSummary: The bill expands when the attorney general’s office may use civil investigative demands, which are formal written requests for records, questions, or testimony. It lets the office use them in certain possible cases involving state or federal law, labor pay laws, discrimination, jail rules, and related state rules, if an assistant attorney general reviews and approves the demand. It also sets rules for what a demand must say, limits some uses, and says it cannot be used for criminal cases or for federal agencies acting in their official work. It became law as Chapter 243, 2026 Laws, and takes effect on 6/11/2026.

WA-2025-SB5837.title: Concerning guardianship, conservatorship, and other protective arrangements.
WA-2025-SB5837.summary:
The following sections of state law are amended.

General Provisions. Qualification for Appointment as a Guardian or Conservator. The age requirement for appointment is reduced from 21 years of age to an adult, which is defined as an individual at least 18 years of age, or an emancipated individual under 18 years of age.

Filing Fee. In order to not be charged a filing fee, for the appointment of potential guardians who are not a professional guardian or conservator, a requirement is removed that a potential guardian be a relative.

Guardianship of Minor. Notice of Hearing for Appointment of Guardian for Minor. All petitions for appointment of a guardian for a minor shall be heard within 90 days unless extended for good cause. Service of notice required for the parent is to be provided to any known parent instead of providing notice to the adult nearest in kin when there is no parent. When unable to serve notice to a person entitled to service, the court may allow service by alternative means, including mail by the United States Postal Service (USPS), email, text message, social media, or other technologies.

When a petitioner is unable to serve notice to a parent, the court shall appoint a court visitor or guardian ad litem who will report to the court whether the parent cannot be located with due diligence, and whether the parent consents to the guardian for the minor, and investigate any other matter related to the petition as directed by the court. The court visitor or guardian ad litem may assist a minor who is the sole petitioner for the purpose of serving notice. The court shall determine whether to appoint a court visitor or guardian ad litem as soon as possible after the filing of the petition.

Attorney for Minor or Parent. The court may appoint an attorney for a minor, including in modification and termination actions, or when a minor is under the age of 12. The court must appoint an attorney for a minor 12 years of age or older if the parent objects to guardianship and the parent has been appointed an attorney. If the sole petitioner is the minor, the court must appoint an attorney for the minor after receipt of the petition. If the petitioner is not the minor, the court may appoint an attorney for the petitioner if the petitioner is indigent and a party who contests the guardianship has an attorney, or for the efficiency of the proceedings and to ensure the court has sufficient information, or the court determines the petitioner needs representation.

Attendance and Participation at Hearing for Appointment of Guardian for Minor. A minor may also attend other proceedings such as mediation or settlement conferences and participate in the proceedings.

WA-2025-HB2471.title: Concerning collective bargaining for employees not covered by the national labor relations act.
WA-2025-HB2471.summary:
Scope. Employers, employees, trades, or industries that were previously subject to federal labor regulations are placed under the jurisdiction of PERC when:
• federal law ceases to preempt the regulation of private sector labor-management relations in the state for an employer, employee, trade, or industry;
• the NLRB determines that the employer, employee, trade, or industry falls outside the previously existing jurisdiction of the NLRA; or
• the NLRB declines to exercise jurisdiction, or is deprived of its previous jurisdiction, over the employer, employee, trade, or industry.

The bill does not apply to symphony musicians, agricultural cannabis workers, or employers, employees, trades, or industries covered by other state collective bargaining laws.

Employees covered under the bill are any employees of an employer, including consumer directed employers of individual providers, and includes individuals whose work has ceased as a consequence of a labor dispute, and who has not obtained any other regular and substantially equivalent employment.

An employee is not:
• an individual employed by their parent or spouse, unless they are also employed by a third-party for the work performed;
• an individual that is an independent contractor;
• an individual employed as a supervisor;
• a person employed by the state, a political subdivision of the state, or an employee under state statutes related to collective bargaining of symphony musicians or agricultural cannabis workers;
• any individual employed by an employer, trade, or industry that was not under the jurisdiction of the NLRA or any other federal labor relations law as of the effective date of the bill; or
• any other person not employed by an employer.

Certification of Bargaining Representatives. Upon application by a labor organization that was an exclusive bargaining representative under federal law prior to when state regulation of private sector labor relations is no longer preempted, PERC must promptly certify the exclusive bargaining representative under state law. Absent exceptional cause, certification must be completed within one month of the application.

PERC must determine the exclusive bargaining representative through either conducting a cross-check or an election. If only one labor organization is seeking certification as an exclusive bargaining representative and there is no incumbent exclusive bargaining representative, PERC may determine the question concerning representation by conducting a cross-check comparing the bargaining authorization cards against the employment records of the employer. A determination through a cross-check process may be made upon a showing of interest submitted of more than 50 percent of the employees.

Upon the request of a prospective bargaining representative showing written proof of at least 30 percent representation of the employees within the proposed bargaining unit, PERC must hold an election by secret ballot.

WA-2025-HB2350.title: Increasing transparency regarding residential habilitation center compliance with certain federal requirements.
WA-2025-HB2350.summary:
When DSHS receives notice that a RHC is out of compliance with CMS's conditions of participation or requirements, the secretary is to provide notice within ten days of the following:
• the initial statement of deficiencies or other determination of noncompliance, including the reason or reasons for the finding of noncompliance, and a plain language summary of the findings that explains the nature of the noncompliance and its potential impact on residential safety;
• establishment of any plan of correction for the facility; and
• all subsequent determinations regarding the facility's return, or failure to return, to compliance, and any related enforcement action.

This notice is to be prominently posted at the relevant RHC until the violation is corrected to the satisfaction of CMS. The notices must be posted in a place or places in plain view of the residents of the RHC, persons visiting those residents, and any person who inquires about placement in the facility. Posted notices must be in English and all alternative languages that have been requested by residents of the relevant RHC.

Required notices must also be provided in writing or email to additional individuals designated to receive notices from DSHS on behalf of each resident of the relevant RHC. If individuals for which notice must be provided have indicated a preferred language other than English, notice must be provided in the preferred language.

WA-2025-SB6151.title: Concerning dedicated accounts for fees collected for the implementation of environmental programs.
WA-2025-SB6151.summary:
The Laboratory Accreditation Account (Account) is created as an appropriated account. Fees charged by Ecology to environmental laboratories to cover Ecology's costs for laboratory accreditation are directed into the Account. The Account may be used for Ecology's costs related to laboratory accreditation.

Fees charged by Ecology to cover their costs related to landfill methane emissions are directed into the Air Pollution Control Account. The Air Pollution Control Account may be used for Ecology's costs for landfill methane emissions.

WA-2025-SB6184.title: Updating the office of homeless youth program provisions.
WA-2025-SB6184.summary:
Licensed Overnight Youth Shelters .

The provisions for parental notification when a child arrives at a CRC are modified to include an exception to the parental notification requirement when a compelling reason exists, in alignment with the generally applicable provisions for licensed overnight youth shelters.

Housing Stability for Youth in Crisis Program .

The Housing Stability for Youth in Crisis Program is renamed the "Housing Stability for Youth in Courts Program" and its required minimum of six total participating counties is removed. The expiration date for the program is also removed.

Community Support Teams .

The prohibition on a Team engaging with a family member other than the youth if the parent, guardian, or legal custodian objects to the support or assistance that is offered or provided is removed. Youth are eligible for Team assistance if they seek services from an overnight youth shelter, or another organization. The requirement that the youth "enters" services of the organization in order to be eligible for assistance is removed.

Independent Youth Housing Program .

Provisions related to the IYHP are modified to:
• remove the subcontractor organization administrative cost cap of 12 percent of the total estimated grant amount;
• add costs associated with providing transitional housing to the list of uses for grant funding by subcontractor organizations; and
• remove the requirement that all housing stipends, security deposits, and first and last month's rent stipends must be payable only to a landlord or housing manager of any type of independent housing.

Other Changes .

The statutory definition of "child," "juvenile," "youth," or "minor" for purposes of OHY programs is modified to specify that homeless young adults under age 21 who are residing in a transitional living program for unaccompanied homeless youth at the time they reach age 18 may be considered children for the purpose of continued placement in group care facilities. Emancipated minors may be considered young adults for purposes of eligibility for OHY-administered programs.

The grant funds issued by the OHY that are used to provide flexible financial assistance may be provided directly to eligible youth and young adults or a third party vendor such as a landlord in order to promote housing stability of the program participant.

The term "street youth" is replaced with "unaccompanied homeless youth," and statutory definitions of "homeless" are aligned throughout statutes governing OHY-administered programs.

References to the Department of Social and Health Services are amended to properly refer to the Department of Children, Youth, and Families.

Definitions of "HOPE Center" are aligned across statutes.

WA-2025-SB5936.title: Concerning prevention of and remedies for human trafficking.
WA-2025-SB5936.summary:
Entity Liability. A business entity may be prosecuted when the business entity:
• knowingly engages in human trafficking or coercion of involuntary servitude; or
• does not effectively stop an employee or agent from engaging in conduct constituting human trafficking when the conduct is part of a pattern of human trafficking or coercion of involuntary servitude for the benefit of the entity which the entity knew was occurring.

When a business entity is prosecuted for human trafficking or coercion of involuntary servitude, the court may order the following additional penalties:
• a fine not more than $1 million per offense;
• disgorgement of profits from human trafficking or coercion of involuntary servitude activity; and
• debarment from state and local government contracts.

Victim Confidentiality. Law enforcement officers and prosecuting agencies shall keep confidential the identity, pictures, and images of a victim and the victim’s family in a human trafficking or coercion of involuntary servitude investigation, except to the extent that disclosure is necessary for investigation or prosecution, required by law or court order, or to ensure services or benefits to the victim and the victim’s family.

The identity, pictures, and images of a victim and the victim’s family in a human trafficking or coercion of involuntary servitude investigation is exempt from public inspection and copying under the Public Records Act.

T and U Nonimmigrant Visas. A state or local law enforcement agency, prosecutor, administrative judge, hearing office, or other authority certifying agency that has responsibility for the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity shall as soon as practicable, on the request of an individual who is believed to be a victim of human trafficking or other criminal offense that would qualify the victim for a T or U nonimmigrant visa:
• provide completed and signed T or U nonimmigrant visa certification forms to such persons; and
• ask a federal law enforcement officer to request continued presence.

An individual determined to not meet the requirements of a T or U nonimmigrant visa will be informed of the reason and may make another request and submit additional evidence to satisfy the requirements.
